title: Syllabus
text:
This course introduces students to the foundations of data science and visualization as tools for making sense of complex social, economic, and environmental questions. Students will learn what data are, where they come from, and how different data types shape the kinds of questions we can ask and answer. Using the R programming language as the primary tool, students will practice cleaning, transforming, and organizing data for analysis, with an emphasis on reproducible workflows and clear documentation. While the course focuses on R, students will also be introduced to alternative software commonly used for data work, such as Python, Stata, Tableau, and Excel.
The course highlights best practices for visualizing data, guiding students through the creation of effective charts, graphs, and maps that communicate clearly to a range of audiences. Students will be introduced to spatial data and basic cartographic principles, using R to create maps that illuminate patterns across communities and places. Throughout the semester, students will practice telling evidence-based stories with data, critically evaluating how visual choices influence interpretation, trust, and decision-making in public and professional contexts.
A core component is a semester-long applied project delivered to an external community partner (see Community Partner).

title: Syllabus
text:
Student Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

Develop fluency with core concepts in data, including data types, common sources of quantitative and spatial data, and key issues related to data quality and ethics.
Build practical skills in R for data wrangling, including importing, cleaning, transforming, and reshaping data, as well as writing reusable code to automate repetitive data tasks.
Design and critique static visualizations using principles of visual perception, clarity, and accessibility, focusing on how to match chart types to questions and audiences.
Work with spatial data in R to produce maps and other spatial visualizations that effectively communicate patterns across geographic units and communities.
Construct short, data-driven narratives that integrate text, tables, and graphics to communicate findings to non-technical stakeholders.

What Does This Class Look Like?

Class Format
We meet once a week for three hours in Morrill Hall 005, a basement computer lab, so you don’t need to bring your own computer if you’d rather not. Each class period is built around a central theme, and our time is split between lecture, live coding, and hands-on lab work. Expect the balance to shift toward lab time as the semester goes on and the NBRC project takes over. I’ll build in a break (or two) to divide the three hours into distinct chunks.


Attendance Policy
You are required to attend class. Put simply, class is better—and your project team is more functional—when everyone shows up. Starting in Week 2, I will take attendance every class period. Everyone gets one free absence. Beyond that, absences will cost you points on your participation & attendance grade. If you know you’ll miss a class, give me a heads-up in advance rather than after the fact.


General Classroom Expectations
My goal as your instructor is to be supportive and build a learning environment where you can thrive. Your role as a student is to actively engage with the material, contribute to your project team, manage your time well, and embrace opportunities for hands-on practice. This is a lab-heavy course: you learn R by writing R, not by watching it get written. You’re in charge of your own learning, but you’re never doing it alone.

  mutate(metro = if_else(inmetro == 1, "Metro", "Nonmetro")) |>

  labs(title = "Nonmetro counties are poorer in every Midwest state",
       subtitle = "Average county poverty rate, 2000",

       caption = "Source: ggplot2::midwest") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

title: Week 7: Visual Communication + Launching the NBRC Project
text:
Writing Figures for NBRC

One figure, one message. If a figure needs two sentences to explain, it’s probably two figures.
The title is the takeaway. “Rent burden by county” is a label, while “Nearly half of renters in Addison County pay more than 30% of income on rent” is a finding.
Plain-language labels with units. No column names, no acronyms NBRC staff would have to look up.
Sort categories by value (not A-Z) unless the order itself means something
Label directly when you can, so readers don’t bounce between the figure and a legend
Normalize: per capita, per household, or a percentage, so big counties don’t win every comparison by default
Always cite the source and year in the caption
Sometimes the answer is just a table or a single number. Less can be more.

Not Even Close


One linear trend, one curve, one outlier dragging the line, and one single point doing all the work
Summary statistics are a compression. A chart is often the fastest way to see what the compression might’ve overlooked.
These four charts came from a few lines of ggplot2 code. By the end of tonight you’ll be able to write them yourself, starting with how ggplot2 thinks about a chart.

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Every ggplot Has Three Parts



Data: a data frame, one row per observation (this is why we pivot_longer)
Aesthetics aes(): which columns map to which visual properties, like x position, y position, color, or size
Geoms: the shapes that actually get drawn, like points, bars, lines, or boxes

Everything else (facets, scales, labels, themes) refines those three. R4DS Ch. 9 calls this a layered grammar, because you build a plot by adding layers with +

  geom_point()



base_plot already holds the data and aesthetics. + geom_point() adds the layer that draws one point per row.
base_plot itself hasn’t changed. To keep the new version, assign it: scatter <- base_plot + geom_point().
A first look: more college grads, somewhat less poverty, but lots of scatter

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
section: Mapping a Third Variable to Color
text:
Mapping a Third Variable to Color

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty, color = state)) +
  geom_point()



Anything inside aes() is mapped to a column, and ggplot builds the legend for you
Five colors is about the limit before a chart gets hard to read

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Mapping vs. Setting
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = inmetro))
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")



















Left, mapped: inside aes(), color comes from a column, with a legend
Right, set: outside aes(), one fixed color and no legend
inmetro is stored as a number, so ggplot gives it a 0-to-1 color gradient even though it’s only ever 0 or 1
Rule of thumb: inside aes() if it depends on the data

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Layers Can Stack

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x)



Each + geom_*() adds a layer on top of the last
alpha makes points semi-transparent, so overlapping points show up darker
geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds a linear trend with a confidence band (se = FALSE hides it)

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Global vs. Local Aesthetics

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = state), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, color = "black")



Aesthetics in ggplot() apply to every layer
Aesthetics in a single geom apply only to that layer
Here, color by state for the points, but one overall trend line. Move color = state up into ggplot() and you’d get five lines instead.

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Facets: Small Multiples

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ state)



facet_wrap() makes one panel per value of a variable, all on the same scales
Often easier to read than five colors crammed into one panel

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Labels Make It Readable

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#007155") +
  labs(
    title = "More college grads, less poverty",
    subtitle = "Midwestern counties, 2000 Census",
    x = "Adults with a college degree (%)",
    y = "Population below poverty line (%)",
    caption = "Source: ggplot2::midwest"
  )



Column names like percbelowpoverty are fine for you. They are not fine for anyone else.
A title that states the finding does more work than one that restates the axes

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
The Template

ggplot(data = <DATA>, aes(<MAPPINGS>)) +
  <GEOM_FUNCTION>() +
  <MORE LAYERS, FACETS, LABELS>


Almost every chart this semester, maps included, fits this shape
R4DS Ch. 9 has the full list of geoms, and the ggplot2 cheat sheet is worth keeping open

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text: Break?

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
What Is EDA?

“Far better an approximate answer to the right question, which is often vague, than an exact answer to the wrong question, which can always be made precise.”
— John Tukey


Exploratory data analysis is a loop, not a formal procedure:

Ask a question about your data
Answer it with a chart, a transformation, or a summary
Use what you learned to ask a better question

Most of these charts are for you. They don’t need titles or polish.

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Asking Good Questions

As Wickham says in Ch. 10, “EDA is fundamentally a creative process. And like most creative processes, the key to asking quality questions is to generate a large quantity of questions.”
R4DS Ch. 10 frames it around two kinds of questions: how does a variable vary, and how do variables covary?

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Continuous Variables: Histograms

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)



A histogram cuts the x-axis into bins and counts the rows in each
Most counties sit between about 7% and 18% in poverty, with a tail to the right

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Bin Width Changes the Story
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10)



















Too narrow and it’s noise. Too wide and the shape disappears.
Try a few. There’s no single right answer, and the default (30 bins) is not always the best one.

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
section: Skewed Data: Try a Log Scale
text:
Skewed Data: Try a Log Scale
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = poptotal)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = poptotal)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma())



















Left: Cook County (Chicago, 5M people) squashes everything else into one bar
Right: on a log scale, each step on the axis is ten times bigger than the last, and the distribution becomes readable
County populations, incomes, and housing prices almost always need this

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Categorical Variables: Bar Charts

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = state)) +
  geom_bar()



geom_bar() counts rows for you, the same thing count(state) did in Week 2
If you already have the counts in a column, you can use geom_col() instead, with the counts as y

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Unusual Values

high_poverty <- midwest_df |>
  filter(percbelowpoverty > 30) |>
  select(county, state, poptotal, percbelowpoverty)

high_poverty

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  county    state poptotal percbelowpoverty
  <chr>     <chr>    <int>            <dbl>
1 ALEXANDER IL       10626             32.2
2 PULASKI   IL        7523             30.2
3 MENOMINEE WI        3890             48.7



The long right tail from the histogram, pulled out with filter()
Outliers aren’t automatically errors. Check whether each one is real or a data problem. These are real: Menominee County, WI is almost entirely the Menominee Reservation, and Alexander and Pulaski are at Illinois’s rural southern tip.
Don’t delete an unusual value just because it’s unusual. If it’s a real error, replace it with NA and say so.

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Adding a Column We’ll Reuse

midwest_df <- midwest_df |>
  mutate(metro = if_else(inmetro == 1, "Metro", "Nonmetro"))

midwest_df |> count(metro)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  metro        n
  <chr>    <int>
1 Metro      150
2 Nonmetro   287



inmetro’s 1s and 0s make poor labels, so we add a readable metro column
Assigning back to midwest_df overwrites it with the new version. Every chart from here on can use metro without repeating the mutate().
Overwriting an object is fine for adding a column. Be careful doing it with filter(), since dropped rows don’t come back until you rerun the earlier code.

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Categorical + Continuous: Boxplots

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = metro, y = percollege)) +
  geom_boxplot()



The box is the middle 50% of counties, the line is the median, and the dots are outliers
Metro counties have a clearly higher share of college grads, and far more spread

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Reordering Categories

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = fct_reorder(state, percbelowpoverty, median),
                    y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL)



By default ggplot puts categories in alphabetical order, which is almost never what you want
fct_reorder() sorts them by the median of another variable, so the pattern reads left to right

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Two Categorical Variables

metro_counts <- midwest_df |>
  count(state, metro)

ggplot(metro_counts, aes(x = state, y = metro, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white", size = 6)



count() the combinations first and save them as metro_counts, then draw a tile for each row of it
A heat map like this is really just a colored table. For a handful of categories, a plain table from count() can work just as well.

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Two Continuous Variables

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = popdensity, y = percollege)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x)



The scatterplot you already know, with a log x-axis for the same reason as before
method = "loess" fits a curve instead of a straight line. It’s flat across rural counties, climbs through the middle, and levels off in the densest ones. A straight line would miss that shape.

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Patterns Are Questions, Not Answers
When you spot a pattern, ask:

Could it be coincidence?
How strong is it, and how would you describe it in one sentence?
What other variable might explain it? (Here, metro status is doing a lot of the work.)
Does it hold within subgroups, like each state or metro vs. nonmetro?

EDA points you toward the story. It doesn’t prove it.
Note: There are often many ways to accomplish the same task. Check out this article about alternatives to boxplots.

title: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis & ggplot2
text:
Saving a Plot

p <- ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point()

ggsave("poverty_college.png", p, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)


Same idea as base_plot earlier: save the plot as an object, then hand that object to ggsave()
ggsave() writes it to a file, sized in inches. Set the size on purpose so text doesn’t come out tiny.
Inside a Quarto document, you usually don’t need this. The chart renders right into the HTML.

text:
Tonight’s Data: midwest

437 counties in IL, IN, MI, OH and WI, from the 2000 Census
Comes with the tidyverse (inside ggplot2), so there’s nothing to download
It’s the same shape as your HW2 data: one row per county
Useful columns: county, state, poptotal, percollege, percbelowpoverty, and inmetro (1 = metro county, 0 = non-metro)

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text: Break?

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
How Every dplyr Verb Works

The first argument is always a data frame
The other arguments say what to do with it, using column names without quotes
The result is always a new data frame
The original is left unchanged. To keep a result, assign it with <-.

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
filter(): Keep Rows That Match

midwest |>
  filter(state == "WI", inmetro == 0) |>
  select(county, state, poptotal, inmetro)

# A tibble: 52 × 4
  county   state poptotal inmetro
  <chr>    <chr>    <int>   <int>
1 ADAMS    WI       15682       0
2 ASHLAND  WI       16307       0
3 BARRON   WI       40750       0
4 BAYFIELD WI       14008       0
5 BUFFALO  WI       13584       0
# ℹ 47 more rows


A comma between conditions means and.

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
filter(): Comparisons



Operator
Meaning




==
equals (two = signs!)


!=
does not equal


>, >=, <, <=
greater/less than


&, |
and, or


%in%
matches any value in a list




midwest |> filter(state == "MI" | state == "OH")
midwest |> filter(state %in% c("MI", "OH"))   # same thing, less typing

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
filter(): Mistakes Everyone Makes

midwest |> filter(state = "WI")          # one = sign
midwest |> filter(state == WI)           # forgot the quotes
midwest |> filter(state == "wi")         # capitalization matters
midwest |> filter(state == "WI" | "MI")  # has to be state == "MI"


The first one needs a double equals sign.

A single = sets something, like an argument (digits = 0) or a new column in mutate().
A double == asks a question, “is this equal to that?”, and answers TRUE or FALSE for every row. filter() needs the question.

The last one looks like it should work, but R needs a full comparison on each side of |. Use %in% instead.

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
arrange(): Sort Rows


Default: smallest first

midwest |>
  arrange(percbelowpoverty) |>
  select(county, state, percbelowpoverty)

  county     state percbelowpoverty

2 DU PAGE    IL                2.71

4 WASHINGTON WI                3.24

midwest |>
  arrange(desc(percbelowpoverty)) |>
  select(county, state, percbelowpoverty)

text:
slice(): Pick Rows by Position


slice(): rows by number

midwest |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  select(county, state, poptotal)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  county    state poptotal
  <chr>     <chr>    <int>
1 ADAMS     IL       66090

slice_sample(): random rows

midwest |>
  slice_sample(n = 3) |>

  county   state poptotal

slice_head(n = 5) and slice_tail(n = 5): the first or last 5 rows
slice_sample() gives different rows every time you run it
Position depends on order, so arrange() then slice_head() gives you a “top 5.” slice_max() and slice_min() do that in one step (more on those after the break).

distinct() and count()


distinct(): just the unique values

midwest |> distinct(state)

# A tibble: 5 × 1
  state
  <chr>
1 IL   
2 IN   
3 MI   
4 OH

midwest |> count(state)

  state     n
  <chr> <int>
1 IL      102
2 IN       92
3 MI       83

select(): Keep Some Columns

midwest |>
  select(county, state, starts_with("perc"))

# A tibble: 437 × 15
  county    state percwhite percblack percamerindan percasian percother
  <chr>     <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 ADAMS     IL         96.7     2.58          0.148    0.377     0.188 
2 ALEXANDER IL         66.4    32.9           0.179    0.452     0.0847

#   percpovertyknown <dbl>, percbelowpoverty <dbl>,

Pick columns by name, or with helpers like starts_with(), ends_with(), and contains()
A minus sign drops columns: select(-PID)
You can also use column numbers (called indexes): select(1, 2:5)

text:
rename() and relocate()

midwest |>
  rename(metro = inmetro, pop = poptotal) |>
  relocate(metro, .after = state) |>
  select(county:pop)

# A tibble: 437 × 5
  county    state metro  area   pop
  <chr>     <chr> <int> <dbl> <int>
1 ADAMS     IL        0 0.052 66090
2 ALEXANDER IL        0 0.014 10626
3 BOND      IL        0 0.022 14991
4 BOONE     IL        1 0.017 30806
5 BROWN     IL        0 0.018  5836
# ℹ 432 more rows



rename(new_name = old_name)
relocate() moves columns without dropping any
Why the dot in .after? Most arguments to dplyr verbs are your column names, so dplyr puts a . in front of its own settings (.after, .before, .by) to keep the two from colliding. If your data had a column called after, then relocate(after) would still mean that column.

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
mutate(): Make New Columns

midwest |>
  mutate(
    pop_thousands = poptotal / 1000,
    metro_label = if_else(inmetro == 1, "Metro", "Non-metro")
  ) |>
  select(county, state, pop_thousands, metro_label)

# A tibble: 437 × 4
  county    state pop_thousands metro_label
  <chr>     <chr>         <dbl> <chr>      
1 ADAMS     IL            66.1  Non-metro  
2 ALEXANDER IL            10.6  Non-metro  
3 BOND      IL            15.0  Non-metro  
4 BOONE     IL            30.8  Metro      
5 BROWN     IL             5.84 Non-metro  
# ℹ 432 more rows

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
if_else(): Pick Between Two Values

if_else(inmetro == 1, "Metro", "Non-metro")


if_else() takes 3 arguments, in this order:

a condition: a test that’s TRUE or FALSE for each row
the value to use where the condition is TRUE
the value to use where the condition is FALSE

Here, R checks each county one at a time: if inmetro == 1 is TRUE, the new column gets "Metro"; if it’s FALSE, it gets "Non-metro"
You’ll also see base R’s ifelse() (no underscore) online. It works the same way, but if_else() is stricter and catches more mistakes.

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
case_when(): More Than Two Outcomes







For reference


We won’t use case_when() again in class, but it’s here for when you need it.







midwest |>
  mutate(
    size = case_when(
      poptotal >= 100000 ~ "Large",
      poptotal >= 25000 ~ "Medium",
      .default = "Small"
    )
  ) |>
  count(size)




# A tibble: 3 × 2
  size       n
  <chr>  <int>
1 Large     85
2 Medium   198
3 Small    154




Each line is condition ~ value. Read the ~ as “then”.
R checks the lines top to bottom for each row, and the first TRUE wins. That’s why "Medium" doesn’t need & poptotal < 100000.
.default catches everything that didn’t match (another dot argument!)

text:
group_by() + summarize()

midwest |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(
    counties = n(),
    total_pop = sum(poptotal),
    avg_poverty = mean(percbelowpoverty)

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  state counties total_pop avg_poverty
  <chr>    <int>     <int>       <dbl>
1 IL         102  11430602        13.1
2 IN          92   5544159        10.3
3 MI          83   9295297        14.2
4 OH          88  10847115        13.0
5 WI          72   4891769        11.9



group_by() doesn’t change what you see. It changes what happens next.
summarize() collapses each group down to one row

Grouping by Two Things

midwest |>
  group_by(state, inmetro) |>
  summarize(avg_poverty = mean(percbelowpoverty), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 10 × 3
  state inmetro avg_poverty
  <chr>   <int>       <dbl>
1 IL          0       14.4 
2 IL          1        9.56
3 IN          0       10.8 
4 IN          1        9.59
5 MI          0       15.5 
# ℹ 5 more rows


A question we might have: is non-metro poverty higher than metro poverty in every state?

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
Watch Out: Averaging Averages (or Percentages)
mean(percbelowpoverty) treats a county of 1,700 people the same as Cook County (5 million). To get the real state-wide rate, add up the people, then divide:

midwest |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(
    poverty_rate = sum(poptotal * percbelowpoverty / 100) / sum(poptotal) * 100
  )

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  state poverty_rate
  <chr>        <dbl>
1 IL            11.9
2 IN            10.7
3 MI            13.1
4 OH            12.5
5 WI            10.7


This is where data and coding collide, and it will come up again with the NBRC data.

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
Missing Values

Real data has gaps. In R, a missing value is NA.
Any math with an NA in it returns NA, unless you tell R to skip them


mean(c(10, 20, NA))

[1] NA

mean(c(10, 20, NA), na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 15



midwest has no missing values, but your BEA data might. The HW2 ‘starter code’ handles most of it.

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse
text:
Dropping Missing Values: is.na()

To drop rows with a missing value, use is.na(). The ! means “not”.


town_income <- tibble(
  town = c("Burlington", "Montpelier", "St. Albans"),
  income = c(52000, NA, 61000)
)

town_income |> filter(!is.na(income))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  town       income
  <chr>       <dbl>
1 Burlington  52000
2 St. Albans  61000



filter(income == NA) doesn’t work. Nothing is ever “equal to” a missing value, so always use is.na().

Saving What You Make

rural_wi <- midwest |>
  filter(state == "WI", inmetro == 0)

nrow(midwest)

[1] 437

nrow(rural_wi)

[1] 52



Without <-, the result prints and then disappears

title: Week 2: Into the Tidyverse

A Few Rules (More Like Guidelines)

# hard to read
df2<-midwest|>filter(state=="WI",inmetro==0)|>mutate(PopK=poptotal/1000)

# easier
rural_wi <- midwest |>
  filter(state == "WI", inmetro == 0) |>

Names in snake_case, and names that describe the contents
Spaces around <-, ==, +, and after commas
One verb per line, with |> at the end of each line
Comments explain why, not what

Deliverable Format
Each of the four graded milestones below builds directly on the last. There’s no single “project” handed in at the end, just a steady accumulation of the same deliverable getting more complete and more polished.

Scope & Team Charter (due Oct. 25, 10%)
A short planning document, not an analysis. At this point in the semester, teams have core R/tidyverse skills but haven’t yet covered spatial analysis (Weeks 9–10) and are just starting the Quarto unit (Week 8). Should include:

Team roster and a rough division of responsibilities
The domain area (Rural Housing or Rural Hub Services) and 2–3 concrete research questions the team plans to answer for NBRC
A first pass at data sources (ACS, BLS, USDA ERS, TIGER shapefiles, possible NBRC-provided data)
A work plan mapped to the remaining milestones below

Submit one charter per team: a Quarto document (.qmd) rendered to PDF with format: typst in the YAML header, with one copy of the PDF emailed to the instructor per team. The point at this stage is alignment within the team and with the instructor, not production value.


Preliminary Outputs + Peer Critique (Week 12, 20%)
By this point teams have covered spatial analysis and Quarto, so this milestone should look like real, if rough, output. Expect to bring:

At least one polished chart or map addressing one of your research questions, built in R (ggplot2/sf)
A short written or verbal framing of what the visualization shows and why it matters to NBRC
Participation in structured peer critique, giving and receiving feedback with at least one other team in class

This is graded on effort and communication quality, not on having “finished” analysis. The critique is meant to catch problems while there’s still time to fix them.


Draft Deliverable + Revision (Week 14, 20%)
A near-complete version of the final deliverable: full narrative structure, multiple visualizations/maps, and a clear throughline connecting data to a recommendation or insight for NBRC. Submitted for instructor feedback, with in-class time for revision afterward. Should be built in Quarto, with the team’s choice of a slide deck or a dashboard, consistent with what’s covered in Week 8.


Final Deliverable + Presentation (Week 16, 20%)
This is the polished, NBRC-facing version of the Draft Deliverable, incorporating Week 14 feedback. It’s a Quarto-rendered slide deck or dashboard that could credibly be handed to NBRC staff. Delivered in person in Montpelier alongside a short team presentation to NBRC stakeholders. All teams follow the same general structure so the final outputs can be assembled into one unified product across domain areas.

title: Week 1: What is Data Science?
text:
Types of Data

Quantitative: measured with numbers; answers “how many?” or “how often?”

Continuous: fractions make sense (3.14 miles)
Discrete: fractions don’t make sense (3.14 students)

Qualitative: describes attributes or properties

Nominal: categories with no order (urban / rural)
Ordinal: categories with a ranking (never / sometimes / always)

title: Week 1: What is Data Science?

Primary vs. Secondary Data

Primary data: you collected it yourself
Secondary data: someone else collected it, and you’re using it
Rule of thumb: if you have to ask, it’s secondary data
Almost everything we touch this semester, the ACS, Census, USDA ERS, and any data NBRC hands us, is secondary. Knowing where it came from and how it was collected matters as much as what it says.

text:
Wide vs. Long Data

bea_wide <- tibble(
  county_name = c("Addison, VT", "Chittenden, VT", "Rutland, VT"),
  pop_2020 = c(37363, 168323, 60572),
  pop_2021 = c(37162, 169660, 60381),
  pop_2022 = c(36777, 170533, 59949)
)

bea_wide

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  county_name    pop_2020 pop_2021 pop_2022
  <chr>             <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Addison, VT       37363    37162    36777
2 Chittenden, VT   168323   169660   170533
3 Rutland, VT       60572    60381    59949



One row per county, but each year gets its own column
This is what you get if you ever download multiple years from BEA at once, instead of the single year HW2 asked for

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
pivot_longer(): Wide to Long

bea_long <- bea_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("pop_"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_prefix = "pop_",
    values_to = "population"
  )

bea_long

# A tibble: 9 × 3
  county_name    year  population
  <chr>          <chr>      <dbl>
1 Addison, VT    2020       37363
2 Addison, VT    2021       37162
3 Addison, VT    2022       36777
4 Chittenden, VT 2020      168323
5 Chittenden, VT 2021      169660
# ℹ 4 more rows



One row per county and year, instead of one row per county
Almost everything in dplyr and ggplot2 wants data in this shape
names_prefix strips "pop_" so the year column just holds the number

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
pivot_wider(): The Reverse

bea_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = population)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  county_name    `2020` `2021` `2022`
  <chr>           <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Addison, VT     37363  37162  36777
2 Chittenden, VT 168323 169660 170533
3 Rutland, VT     60572  60381  59949



Takes values from one column and spreads them into new columns, one per unique value
Good for a summary table you want to read by eye, less useful once you need to filter or group by year again

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
Where Data Comes From



A file someone hands you, or you download: CSV, Excel, and the like
A live API (application programming interface) you query with code
A web page you scrape, when nothing else is available
R4DS Ch. 7-8 covers the first in depth. APIs and scraping are in R4DS Ch. 24, much further along in the book than we’ve gotten.
Reading files is readr’s job, the tidyverse package behind read_csv() and other similar functions

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
Reading Files, Revisited

read_csv(
  "data/hw2a.csv",
  skip = 3,
  na = c("", "NA", "(NA)", "N/A")
)


read_csv() is in HW2’s starter code
skip jumps past header rows a file doesn’t need, common in government exports
na tells readr which strings actually mean “missing.” This varies widely.
readr prints a column specification when it loads. Always glance at it. A date or number read in as text usually means a stray character snuck into that column.

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
What’s an API?

Application programming interface: structured way to ask a website for data and get back something other than a webpage, usually JSON
You build a URL with your request baked in, and the server sends back data instead of a rendered page
Census, BLS, and BEA all publish APIs. Some want a free registration key, a few don’t.

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
Not Every API Is Free

There is an entire industry based around data for purchase. For example, you might want to get a drive distance from UVM campus to 500 different addresses in Vermont. You could get this for free by manually entering the addresses into Google Maps. Or you could give Google a single file with every address and have it calculate all 500 distances in a few minutes.
The catch: you have to pay! (a fraction of a penny for each, but it adds up).
If a private data provider gives you an API key, keep it secret or bad actors can drain your credits (or wallet) in a very short time.

title: Week 3: Getting Data
section: A Live Example: the BLS API
text:
A Live Example: the BLS API

library(jsonlite)

url <- "https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/LNS14000000"
bls_raw <- fromJSON(url)
bls_raw

bls_raw$Results$series$data[[1]] |> head()


LNS14000000 is the BLS series ID for the national unemployment rate
No key needed for a request this small, heavier use wants a free one
fromJSON() already turned the nested JSON into data frames. We just have to dig through the list to find the one we want.
Read bls_raw$Results$series$data[[1]] left to right: start at bls_raw, step into $Results, then $series, then grab the first item out of the data list with [[1]]

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
Web Scraping: A Quick Look

library(rvest)

page <- read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_counties_in_Vermont")
counties <- page |>
  html_element("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table()


Some data only exists inside a web page, with no file or API behind it
rvest reads a page’s HTML and pulls out a specific table or element
The process is fragile: if the page’s layout changes, your code breaks with no warning
Use it last, after checking for a file or an API. Read the site’s terms of service and robots.txt first, and never hit a server with rapid repeated requests, it can look like an attack and get you blocked.

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
Why Joins

HW2 step 5 asks you to combine df and df2 using a shared column, county_fips
A join lines up rows from two tables using one or more shared columns, called keys (we will often refer to this as a “unique identifier”)
Nothing here is BEA-specific. Joins work the same way on any two data frames that share a key.

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
A Small Example

pop <- tibble(
  county_fips = c("50001", "50003", "50007"),
  county_name = c("Addison", "Bennington", "Chittenden"),
  population = c(37363, 34478, 168323)
)

income <- tibble(
  county_fips = c("50001", "50003", "50011"),
  income = c(58000, 52000, 71000)
)


Both tables share county_fips, the key
The counties don’t fully overlap: 50007 is only in pop, 50011 only in income

title: Week 3: Getting Data
section: left_join(): Keep Everything on the Left
text:
left_join(): Keep Everything on the Left

pop |> left_join(income, by = "county_fips")

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  county_fips county_name population income
  <chr>       <chr>            <dbl>  <dbl>
1 50001       Addison          37363  58000
2 50003       Bennington       34478  52000
3 50007       Chittenden      168323     NA



Every row of pop survives, matched or not
Chittenden (50007) has no match in income, so it gets NA
50011’s income is dropped. It wasn’t in pop to begin with.

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
Other Join Types, Briefly



Join
Keeps




left_join()
Everything on the left, matched where possible


inner_join()
Only rows that match in both


full_join()
Everything from both, matched where possible



left_join() is the one you’ll reach for almost every time: you have a main table and you’re adding to it.

title: Week 3: Getting Data
text:
Watch Out: Duplicate Column Names

If both tables have a column with the same name that isn’t the key (both have county_name, say), the join keeps both and adds .x and .y suffixes
Two fixes:

select() away the extra column from one side before joining
Join on every shared column: by = c("county_fips", "county_name", "state")

text:
Tonight’s Data

midwest_df <- midwest |>
  select(county, state, poptotal, popdensity, percollege,
         percbelowpoverty, inmetro) |>
  mutate(metro = if_else(inmetro == 1, "Metro", "Nonmetro"))

midwest_df

# A tibble: 437 × 8
  county   state poptotal popdensity percollege percbelowpoverty inmetro
  <chr>    <chr>    <int>      <dbl>      <dbl>            <dbl>   <int>
1 ADAMS    IL       66090      1271.       19.6            13.2        0
2 ALEXAND… IL       10626       759        11.2            32.2        0
3 BOND     IL       14991       681.       17.0            12.1        0
4 BOONE    IL       30806      1812.       17.3             7.21       1
5 BROWN    IL        5836       324.       14.5            13.5        0
# ℹ 432 more rows
# ℹ 1 more variable: metro <chr>



The same 437 Midwestern counties as last week, with the readable metro column already added
We’ll also borrow economics, a second dataset built into ggplot2, because midwest has no time dimension
The template hasn’t changed: data, aesthetics, geoms. Everything tonight is a new piece to plug into it.

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Lines: Change Over Time

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line()



economics has one row per month of US data from 1967 to 2015. unemploy is the number of unemployed people, in thousands.
geom_line() connects the observations in order along the x-axis. Reach for it when x is time.
The peak is 15.4 million people in October 2009

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
One Year, Crowded Axis
unemploy_2009 <- economics |>
  filter(date >= "2009-01-01", date <= "2009-12-01") |>
  mutate(month = month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE))

ggplot(unemploy_2009, aes(x = month, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_col()
ggplot(unemploy_2009, aes(x = month, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))



















2009 was the peak year from the last slide. Twelve full month names at the default angle run into each other.
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) rotates just the x-axis text. hjust keeps the rotated labels lined up under their bars.
Axis text, titles, and ticks are all controlled through theme(), one element_text() at a time

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Bubbles: A Third Variable

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty, size = poptotal)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4)



size is another aesthetic. It maps a number to the area of each point instead of a position or a color.
Bigger circles are more populous counties, and Cook County (Chicago) jumps out immediately
Three numeric variables on one scatterplot, with no new geom. Just one more mapping inside aes().

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Densities: Comparing Distributions

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, fill = metro)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)



A density is a smoothed histogram. It makes two overlapping groups much easier to compare than two stacked histograms.
Each curve has the same area, so 150 metro counties and 287 nonmetro counties can be compared directly
Nonmetro counties bunch up around 15%. Metro counties sit higher and spread much wider.

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Text and Highlighting

high_poverty <- midwest_df |>
  filter(percbelowpoverty > 30) |>
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county))

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(color = "gray70") +
  geom_point(data = high_poverty, color = "#007155", size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = high_poverty, aes(label = county), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1, size = 5)



A layer can use its own data. The gray points are every county, and the green points and labels come from high_poverty (last week’s three unusual values).
geom_text() needs a label aesthetic. hjust and nudge_x move the text off the point.
Gray for context plus one color for the story is one of the most useful tricks in the whole package
When a layer draws from a different data frame than the one in ggplot(), you have to name it with data =. Leave that out and the layer uses midwest_df again.

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Scales: Controlling the Axes

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1),
                     breaks = seq(0, 50, by = 10))



Every aesthetic has a scale, and ggplot picks a default for each. The functions are named scale_<aesthetic>_<type>().
labels controls how the numbers are written and breaks controls where the ticks go
scale = 1 because our data is already 0 to 100. Without it, label_percent() assumes proportions and would print 2,000%.
Other helpers we might want: label_comma() and label_dollar()
scales::label_percent() borrows one function from the scales package without a library(scales) at the top. The package::function() form is handy for a one-off like this.

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
A Quick Note on Color



Today’s colors are placeholders. Color is a design choice like any other, and we’ll come back to it when we cover best practices
Palettes generally come in three types: sequential (low to high), diverging (two directions from a meaningful middle), and qualitative (categories, no order)
Click the screenshot to open the ColorBrewer tool

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Color Scales: Categories

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty, color = metro)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Metro" = "#f35d00", "Nonmetro" = "gray60"))



Color is an aesthetic, so it has a scale too. scale_color_manual() lets you name the color for each category.
Don’t want to pick colors yourself? scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") uses a ready-made palette. Other palletes from Brewer are also available.
Points and lines take color. Bars, boxes, and densities take fill, so their scales are scale_fill_*().

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Color Scales: Continuous Values

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = popdensity, y = percollege, color = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1)



A number mapped to color needs a gradient that runs from light to dark in one direction
The viridis palettes ("viridis", "magma", "plasma", and others) do that, and they stay readable in grayscale and for color-blind readers
direction = -1 flips the palette so that dark means high

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Themes
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_classic()



















A theme controls the background, gridlines, fonts, and legend placement. It never touches the data.
The gray default is theme_gray(). Also built in: theme_bw(), theme_light(), and theme_void() (nothing at all, which is what we’ll use for maps).

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
A Finished Visualization

ggplot(midwest_df, aes(x = percollege, y = percbelowpoverty, color = metro)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Metro" = "#007155", "Nonmetro" = "gray60")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "The most college-educated counties are metro counties",
    subtitle = "Midwestern counties, 2000 Census",
    x = "Adults with a college degree",
    y = "Population below poverty line", 
    color = NULL,
    caption = "Source: ggplot2::midwest"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = 'Tahoma') +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.title = element_text(face = 'bold'))


Nothing new here. It’s tonight’s pieces stacked on last week’s scatterplot: a color scale, two axis scales, labels, and a theme.
theme() adjusts one element at a time, on top of whichever complete theme you chose
Of the 24 counties where more than 30% of adults have a degree, 21 are metro

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
section: You Read Far More Figures Than You Make
text:
You Read Far More Figures Than You Make
Tonight’s reading suggests four questions to ask of any figure, whether it’s yours or someone else’s:

What do you see? Sum up the main takeaway in one sentence.
Who created it? The source often tells you what the figure is for.
Are you being tricked? Look at the axes, the scales, and the sizes.
What is missing? Ask what data or context was left out.

When something is off, Wilke’s three words help you say how it’s off:

Ugly: an aesthetic problem, like clashing colors or distracting fonts
Bad: a perception problem. The figure is hard to read.
Wrong: an accuracy problem. The figure misstates the data.

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Rule 1: Start With the Question
Before picking a geom, ask what you are trying to show. The reading’s decision tree (Figure 1) has four branches, plus maps:

Distribution: how values are spread out (histogram, density, boxplot)
Composition: how a whole divides into parts (stacked bars or a waffle plot, rarely a pie)
Relationship: how variables move together (scatterplot)
Comparison: how groups or time periods differ (bar chart, line chart)
Geography: where something happens (maps, starting in Week 8)

The same data can sit on more than one branch. We’ll spend more time on choosing a chart type in a few weeks.

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Rule 2: Show the Data

“Above all else show the data.”
— Edward Tufte

Tufte’s five principles from The Visual Display of Quantitative Information:

Above all else, show the data
Maximize the data-ink ratio
Erase non-data-ink
Erase redundant data-ink
Revise and edit


Data-ink is the part of a figure that actually represents data. Everything else is non-data-ink: borders, backgrounds, heavy gridlines, and decoration that Tufte calls chartjunk.
You don’t have to be as strict as Tufte. The useful habit is asking of every element, “what is this doing for the reader?”

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Same Five Numbers, Less Ink



















Gone: the legend and the five colors (the axis already names each state), the bar outlines, the gray panel, the border, and the gridlines
Added: the numbers themselves, and an order that means something
Five colors for five bars is redundant data-ink. Color was saying the same thing as position.

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
section: Rule 3: Ink Should Be Proportional to the Data
text:
Rule 3: Ink Should Be Proportional to the Data
ggplot(state_summary, aes(x = state, y = avg_poverty)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(10, 14.5))
ggplot(state_summary, aes(x = state, y = avg_poverty)) +
  geom_col()



















A bar’s length is the number. Cut off the bottom of the axis and the lengths no longer match the data.
Left: Michigan’s bar is about eight times as tall as Indiana’s. Right: the real gap is 14.2% vs. 10.3%, about 38% higher.
Bars start at zero, always. Points and lines encode position rather than length, so they have more freedom, but a tight axis can still exaggerate a small change.

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
section: How to Lie With a Figure
text:
How to Lie With a Figure
recent <- economics |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2010-01-01"))

ggplot(recent, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line()
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line()



















Every number in both plots is true. Left: unemployment is in free fall. Right: same five years are the recovery from the highest count in the series.
Tufte: graphics must not quote data out of context. Choosing the start date is one of the easiest ways to do it. 
Even the right-hand plot leaves something out. The US grew from 199M to 320M over these years, so a raw count overstates the trend. Rates > counts (usually).

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Rule 4: Give Color One Job
Wilke describes three uses of color. Pick one per figure:

Distinguish categories: a qualitative palette, with no implied order (scale_color_brewer(), scale_color_manual())
Represent values: a sequential palette, light to dark (scale_color_viridis_c())
Highlight: gray for everything, one color for the thing you want seen

And three ways it goes wrong:

Too many categories: beyond three to five colors, readers can’t keep track. Facet or highlight instead.
Color for the sake of color: if the color doesn’t encode anything, it’s decoration
The wrong kind of palette for the data, which is the next two slides

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
A Rainbow Has No Order

Diverging Palettes Need a Real Midpoint
color_plot + scale_color_distiller(palette = "RdBu")
color_plot + scale_color_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1)



















A diverging palette has two colors that meet at a neutral middle. It tells the reader there are two kinds of values, above and below.
Left: the middle lands near 25% poverty only because that’s halfway between the lowest and highest county. Nothing actually happens at 25%.
Use diverging colors when the midpoint means something, like zero change, a break-even point, or a national average. Otherwise use a sequential palette.

title: Week 5: More ggplot2 + Best Practices in Data Visualization
text:
Rule 5: Know Who’s Reading

Color-vision deficiency: roughly 1 in 12 men (~1 in 200 women) can’t reliably tell red from green. Viridis and the ColorBrewer palettes marked colorblind-safe are built for this.
Grayscale: if your figure might be printed or photocopied, check that it survives without color
Connotation: colors carry meaning before your legend does. Red and blue on a US map reads as politics, red reads as hot or bad, and green reads as good.
Normalize: a map or bar chart of raw counts mostly shows where people live. Divide by population, households, or farms so places can be compared.
Expertise: NBRC staff know the region far better than you do, and they are not R users. Titles, labels, and units should need no translation.

The last bullet could be it’s own class. Writing/communicating for non-technical audience is harder than it sounds. Just ask Extension folks!

Before You Share a Visualization

Can you state the takeaway in one sentence? Is that sentence the title?
Does the chart type match the question (distribution, composition, relationship, comparison, geography)?
Do bars start at zero, and are the axes honest and labeled in plain language?
Is color doing exactly one job, with the right kind of palette?
Could a reader be misled by what you left out (the time window, the denominator, the comparison group)?
Is there anything you could erase without losing information?
Would it survive a black-and-white printer?

That’s the big idea of Quarto: you write one plain-text file with your words and your code, and Quarto turns it into whatever format you need. YAML header (between the two --- lines): settings for the whole document
Markdown text: your writing, with light formatting
Code chunks: R code that runs when you render, with the results placed into the document


Every Quarto document has three ingredients. At the top, between the two lines of three dashes, is the YAML header. That’s where settings for the whole document live: the title, the author, the output format. Then there’s ordinary text written in Markdown, which is just a light way of adding formatting, like the two asterisks around “poorer” that make it bold. And then there are code chunks, the gray blocks that start with three backticks and r in curly braces. When you render, Quarto runs that code and drops the results right into the document. That’s it. Everything else is detail.

title: Week 8: Quarto + Storytelling with Data
text:
The YAML Header
---
title: "Rural Poverty in the Midwest"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format: html
embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  message: false
  warning: false
---

YAML (“YAML Ain’t Markup Language”…a programmer joke): a format for settings
Each line is a key: value pair. Indentation matters: two spaces means “this belongs to the line above.”
date: today fills in the date every time you render
embed-resources: true packs the styling and figures into the one .html file. Without it, Quarto puts them in a separate hw3_files folder, and the page looks broken when you open it in Posit Cloud.
execute: sets chunk options for the whole document. Here, it hides all code, messages, and warnings, because the reader is NBRC and not a programmer.
A YAML typo is one of the most common reasons a document won’t render. When something breaks, check the header first.


Replace the header at the top of hw3.qmd with this one, everything between and including the two lines of dashes, and put your own name in. YAML, by the way, stands for “YAML Ain’t Markup Language.” Yes, the acronym contains itself. Programmers think that’s funny. All you need to know is that it’s a simple format for settings. Each line is a key, a colon, and a value. Indentation matters a lot in YAML. Notice that echo, message, and warning are indented two spaces under execute. That’s how YAML knows they belong to execute. date: today just fills in today’s date whenever you render. embed-resources true tells Quarto to pack everything, the fonts, the styling, and the figures, into a single HTML file. Leave that line out and you get a plain, broken-looking page in Posit Cloud, because the styling ends up in a separate folder the viewer doesn’t load. And the execute section is new: it sets options for every code chunk in the document at once. Here we’re saying hide the code, hide the messages, hide the warnings. Why? Because this is a report for a reader who doesn’t care about our code. One practical tip: if a document refuses to render, the YAML is the first place to look. A missing space or a stray tab will break it.

Code Chunks

Insert one with the green +C button above the editor, or Code → Insert Chunk
While you work, run a chunk with the green ▶ in its top-right corner, same as in your homework
Chunk options go at the very top of the chunk, each on a line starting with #|

```{r}
#| label: fig-poverty
#| fig-cap: "Average county poverty rate by state and metro status, 2000."
#| echo: false
ggplot(pov_df, aes(x = avg_poverty, y = state)) +
  geom_point()
```

Code chunks. You can type the three backticks yourself, or click the little green plus-C button at the top of the editor, or use Code, Insert Chunk from the menu. Desktop RStudio has a keyboard shortcut for this, but in a web browser it can collide with the browser’s own shortcuts, so I’d stick with the button. While you’re working, you run a chunk with the green play arrow, just like you have all semester. The new part is chunk options. They go at the very top of the chunk, on lines that start with a pound sign and a vertical bar. These control how the chunk shows up in the rendered document. Let’s look at the ones you’ll use most.

title: Week 8: Quarto + Storytelling with Data
text:
Chunk Options You’ll Actually Use








Option
What it does
Use it for




echo: false
Runs the code, shows only the result
Figures for NBRC


include: false
Runs the code, shows nothing at all
Loading packages and data


message: false
Hides messages
The startup text from library(tidyverse)


warning: false
Hides warnings
Only after you’ve read them!


label: fig-...
Gives a figure a name
Referring to it in your text


fig-cap: "..."
Adds a caption under a figure
Every figure in a deliverable




Put an option under execute: in the YAML to apply it to every chunk. Put it in one chunk to apply it just there.
A chunk’s own option wins. So with echo: false in the YAML, you could still show one chunk’s code with #| echo: true.


Here are the six chunk options worth knowing. echo false runs the code but only shows the result, so you get the figure without the code that made it. include false runs the code and shows nothing at all, which is perfect for a setup chunk where you load packages and data. message false and warning false hide those red messages. A word of caution: read your warnings before you hide them, because sometimes they’re telling you something real. Label gives a chunk a name, and if the label starts with fig-dash you can refer to that figure in your text, which we’ll do in a minute. And fig-cap adds a caption. Any of these can go in the YAML under execute to apply everywhere, or in a single chunk to apply just there, and the chunk’s own setting wins.

section: Inline Code: Numbers That Update Themselves
text:
Inline Code: Numbers That Update Themselves
Below the setup chunk, add a heading and a sentence:
## Bottom Line

**Nonmetro counties are poorer than metro counties in every Midwest state.** Across all `r nrow(midwest)` counties, the average nonmetro county had a poverty rate of `r round(nonmetro_avg, 1)`%, compared with `r round(metro_avg, 1)`% for metro counties.
When you render, the reader sees:
Nonmetro counties are poorer than metro counties in every Midwest state. Across all 437 counties, the average nonmetro county had a poverty rate of 13.7%, compared with 10.3% for metro counties.

Inline code is a backtick, the letter r, a space, any R code, and a closing backtick
Use round() so readers see 13.7%, not 13.668967%
Never type a number from your output into your text by hand. When the data changes (say, a new ACS year), inline numbers update on their own!


This is one of my favorite things about Quarto. Inside a normal sentence, you can drop in a little bit of R code. It’s a backtick, the letter r, a space, your code, and a closing backtick. When you render, Quarto runs that code and puts the result right in the sentence. So instead of me looking at my console, seeing 13.7, and typing 13.7 into my report, the report calculates it. Why does that matter? Because your data will change. You’ll fix a filter, or swap in a newer year of the American Community Survey, and every number in your text updates by itself. Copying numbers by hand is how reports end up saying one thing in the text and another in the figure. Use round so the reader sees one decimal place instead of six.

title: Week 8: Quarto + Storytelling with Data
text:
Figures, Captions, and Cross-References
## The Gap, State by State

```{r}
#| label: fig-poverty
#| fig-cap: "Average county poverty rate by state and metro status, 2000. Source: ggplot2::midwest."
ggplot(pov_df, aes(x = avg_poverty, y = fct_reorder(state, avg_poverty), color = metro)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = state), color = "gray70", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Metro" = "gray50", "Nonmetro" = "#007155")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Nonmetro counties are poorer in every Midwest state",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The gap is widest in Illinois and narrowest in Indiana (@fig-poverty).

A figure’s label must start with fig-
@fig-poverty becomes “Figure 1,” with a clickable link. Add another figure above it and the numbering updates itself.
The title states the finding. The caption says what’s plotted and where the data came from.


Next, add a second section with last week’s dumbbell plot. Two chunk options at the top: a label, fig-poverty, and a caption. The label has to start with fig-dash. That’s how Quarto knows it’s a figure. Then, in your text, you type at-sign fig-poverty, and in the rendered document that becomes “Figure 1,” as a clickable link. If you later add a figure above this one, it becomes Figure 2 everywhere, automatically. Notice how the title and the caption do different jobs. The title is the takeaway, the thing we talked about last week. The caption is the plain description: what’s plotted, what year, and the source.

text:
Follow Along: The Whole File
---
title: "Rural Poverty in the Midwest"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format: html
embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  message: false
  warning: false
---

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

pov_df <- midwest |>
  mutate(metro = if_else(inmetro == 1, "Metro", "Nonmetro")) |>
  group_by(state, metro) |>
  summarize(avg_poverty = mean(percbelowpoverty), .groups = "drop")

metro_avg <- midwest |>
  filter(inmetro == 1) |>
  summarize(avg = mean(percbelowpoverty)) |>
  pull(avg)

nonmetro_avg <- midwest |>
  filter(inmetro == 0) |>
  summarize(avg = mean(percbelowpoverty)) |>
  pull(avg)
```

## Bottom Line

**Nonmetro counties are poorer than metro counties in every Midwest state.** Across all `r nrow(midwest)` counties, the average nonmetro county had a poverty rate of `r round(nonmetro_avg, 1)`%, compared with `r round(metro_avg, 1)`% for metro counties (@fig-poverty).

## The Gap, State by State

```{r}
#| label: fig-poverty
#| fig-cap: "Average county poverty rate by state and metro status, 2000. Source: ggplot2::midwest."
ggplot(pov_df, aes(x = avg_poverty, y = fct_reorder(state, avg_poverty), color = metro)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = state), color = "gray70", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Metro" = "gray50", "Nonmetro" = "#007155")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Nonmetro counties are poorer in every Midwest state",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The gap is widest in Illinois and narrowest in Indiana.

## About the Data

County data come from the `midwest` dataset that ships with ggplot2, based on the 2000 Census. Averages are simple county averages, not weighted by population.

Here’s the whole file in one place. If you got lost anywhere along the way, copy this whole thing into hw3.qmd, replacing everything in it, and change the author to your name. The same file, with the final two-format header, is in your instructions HTML. Notice the last section, About the Data. Everything you hand NBRC should end with something like this: where the data came from, what year, and any caveats a careful reader should know. Here the caveat is that these are simple averages across counties, so a tiny county counts as much as Cook County.

title: Week 8: Quarto + Storytelling with Data
text:
Exploring vs. Explaining

Most of what you’ve done in this course so far is exploring. You make lots of quick figures to find out what’s in the data, and you are the audience.
A deliverable is explaining. You already know what you found, and your job is to get it into someone else’s head quickly.
Your group might end up making dozens of figures for your NBRC project and only show a handful. Choosing which ones is most of the work.


Part three: storytelling. I want to start with a distinction. Almost everything you’ve done in R so far has been exploring. You make a quick plot, look at it, make another one. You’re the audience, and it doesn’t need to be pretty. A deliverable is a completely different job. Now you know the answer, and your job is to get that answer into somebody else’s head as fast as possible. For your project, you’ll probably make dozens of figures and end up showing maybe five. Deciding which five, and in what order, is the actual storytelling.

title: Week 8: Quarto + Storytelling with Data
text:
Bottom Line Up Front

Busy readers, like agency staff and commissioners, look at the title, the first slide or two (or the top of a dashboard), and the figures. Then they stop.
So put the answer first. Don’t make them wait until the end to find out what you found.
A structure that works for a slide deck (and for a short document like HW3):

Bottom line: the finding, in one or two sentences, right after the title
Evidence: one slide (or section) per finding, each built around one figure
What it means: implications for NBRC. What could someone do with this?
About the data: sources, years, and caveats

On a dashboard, same idea: the most important figure or number goes at the top
This is not the shape of a research paper (introduction, literature, methods, results). Write for the reader you actually have.


The single most useful rule I can give you is bottom line up front. Think about who looks at your work at NBRC. They’re busy. They’ll read the title, the first slide or two, maybe look at the figures, and then they’ll move on to the next thing in their inbox. So the answer has to come first. Here’s a structure that works for a slide deck, and for a short document like HW3. Lead with the bottom line, right after the title. Then the evidence, one slide per finding, each built around a figure. Then what it means for NBRC: what decision could someone make with this? And close with a short note about the data. On a dashboard it’s the same idea: the most important figure or number goes at the top, where people look first. Notice that this is the opposite of how a lot of us were trained to write academic papers, where the findings come at the end. That’s fine for a journal. It’s not fine for a partner.

title: Week 8: Quarto + Storytelling with Data
section: Let the Headings Tell the Story
text:
Let the Headings Tell the Story

Slide titles and section headings can be findings too. “Nonmetro counties are poorer in every state” tells the reader more than “Results.”
Figure titles state the takeaway (Week 7). Captions say what’s plotted and where it came from.
Use @fig- references so your text and your figures point at each other
A quick test: read only your slide titles (or headings) and figure titles, in order. If they tell the whole story on their own, your structure works.


Your slide titles and headings are prime real estate. A heading that says “Results” tells the reader nothing. A heading that says “Nonmetro counties are poorer in every state” tells them the finding even if they read nothing else. Same with figure titles, which we talked about last week. Here’s a test I use on my own work: read only the slide titles or headings and the figure titles, in order, and skip everything else. If that skeleton tells the whole story, the structure is working. If it doesn’t, no amount of polishing the paragraphs will fix it.

title: Week 8: Quarto + Storytelling with Data
text:
Every Number Needs Context

“13.7%” means nothing on its own. Compared to what? Metro counties? Ten years ago? The state? The nation?
Round for readers, and name the units and the year every time
Normalize (per capita, per household, or a percentage) so big places don’t win every comparison by default. (this is now the 5th or 6th time I’ve emphasized this!)
Say what the data can’t tell you. Honest caveats build trust with a partner like NBRC.


A few habits about numbers. A number alone doesn’t mean anything. If I tell you the average nonmetro county had a poverty rate of 13.7 percent, your next question should be: compared to what? That’s why our bottom-line sentence gave you the metro number right alongside it. Always round to something a person can hold in their head, and always say the units and the year. Normalize, so you’re comparing rates and not raw counts. And be honest about limits. If your data is from 2020 and things have changed since, say so. NBRC will trust your findings more, not less, when you’re upfront about what the data can’t do.

title: Week 8: Quarto + Storytelling with Data
text:
Hide the Machinery

NBRC staff don’t need your code. Set echo: false, message: false, and warning: false for the whole document.
Keep your exploring in a separate file (like exploration.qmd or even exploration.R) and only the explaining in the deliverable
Plain language: “renters paying more than 30% of income on rent,” not pct_rent_burden
Read it out loud once (or many times) before you share with stakeholders!


Last thing on storytelling: hide the machinery. Your reader doesn’t need to see your code or R’s messages, so turn them off for the whole document. A habit that really helps on a team project is keeping two files: a messy exploration file where you try everything, and a clean deliverable file that only contains what you’re explaining. And use plain language everywhere, including labels. Nobody at NBRC knows what your column names mean. Finally, read it out loud, more than once if you can, before you share it with stakeholders. You’ll hear the awkward sentences right away.
